blurb: Athletic English gundog famed for freezing in a classic point when it scents game
description: The Pointer, or English Pointer, is a medium-sized, athletic British gundog with a short, fine coat, usually white with coloured patches, and an even nature.
answer: The Pointer, sometimes called the English Pointer, is a medium-sized pointing dog developed in England to find game birds and signal their position by standing still and pointing. Kennel Club standards call for about 61 to 69 cm in height, and the breed is described as adaptable, obedient and even-tempered.

body: The most common view is that the Pointer descends from Old Spanish Pointers brought to England in the early 18th century, possibly by soldiers returning after the Peace of Utrecht in 1713, though other sources point to Portuguese, Italian or French pointing dogs. The earliest English records, including a 1713 poem by John Gay and a 1725 painting, date from this period.

Early Pointers were heavy, slow dogs, but as firearms improved, breeders added Greyhound blood for speed, producing the finer modern dog. Crosses with setters, Bloodhounds and Foxhounds are also recorded. The breed standard was formally adopted in 1936 and has changed little since.

The Pointer is athletic and built for speed and endurance, usually weighing 20 to 34 kg. Its distinctive head has a slightly dished face, raised brow and wide nostrils, with high-set hanging ears. The short, fine, hard coat is usually white with lemon, orange, liver or black patches. Field-bred and show-bred lines have diverged noticeably in build.

The breed is commonly described as adaptable, obedient and even-tempered, with field lines in particular extremely active. Compared with other gundogs it is said to be more aloof and reserved, with a lower need for human companionship, possibly reflecting its Greyhound ancestry.

Bred to quarter fast and wide in search of game, the Pointer, especially from working lines, is generally expected to need substantial daily exercise. Its short coat is low-maintenance. It remains the most popular pointing breed on UK sporting estates and US shooting preserves, and is also used in falconry.

The Pointer is considered generally healthy, with a life expectancy of 13 to 14 years, and The Kennel Club does not recommend specific screening tests. Conditions reported in the breed include hip and elbow dysplasia, patellar luxation, hereditary sensory neuropathy, spinal muscular atrophy, X-linked cerebellar ataxia and deafness, with minor predispositions to hypothyroidism, demodicosis and some eye conditions.

faq.a: The breed is considered generally healthy, with a life expectancy of about 13 to 14 years.
A classically trained Pointer points and flushes game but does not usually retrieve it; specialist retrievers are often used for that.

faq.q: Is the Pointer recognised by the FCI?
faq.a: Yes. The FCI lists the English Pointer as breed number 1 in Group 7, with Great Britain as the country of origin.
